Very misleading headline. If Netflix doesn't play under the current rules, they won't be around to push for changing them.

>"We are strong advocates for net neutrality and don't believe data caps are good for consumers and the Internet generally," a Netflix spokesperson told Ars. "That said, such arrangements are common in Australia and we won't put our new members at a disadvantage to those of rival services."

I agree. The article did feel like a "gotcha" piece. But Netflix isn't reversing their opinion, they're just saying "We want to do business in Australia, and while we disagree with the rules, we have to play by the rules in order to do business".

I usually expect better quality reporting from arstechnica.

I'm an iiNet user (with a US Netflix account right now), so I'm all for it, but I can see where they're coming from. I feel like the US and AU ISP environments aren't the exact same, though. They're similar (generally tied to one provider on the backend, although the frontend has different sellers), but the difference is we have had quotas for a long time (10+ years), barring a few technically "unlimited" plans. Most ISPs have free traffic that doesn't use quota, too. Usually it's http/ftp mirrors full of software, but they're starting to provide streaming video. Netflix is coming into the game where the ISP/consumer relationship is in a different situation, and just going with the flow.
